passage: I'm Ayesha. I worked with Lakshmi in the buying team of a big clothing chain in Bengaluru, and I watched her change over a year, though I can't say exactly why. At first she was the best at spotting trends; she would order fifty thousand pieces of a new top and it would sell out. Then after a work trip to the dye units in Tiruppur, she came back quiet. She started bringing lunch in steel boxes and cycling the four kilometres to office. In a meeting she asked how many unsold pieces we burned each season; nobody answered. In March she resigned and took a lower-paid job at a startup that turns textile waste into insulation. At her farewell she only said, "I want my work to leave less behind." Some people rolled their eyes. I noticed I'd started checking the labels on my own clothes.

qa.q: How far did Lakshmi cycle to office?
qa.a: Four kilometres.

qa.q: What might Lakshmi have been feeling after the trip to the dye units?
qa.a: Lakshmi seemed troubled and thoughtful, coming back quiet, though Ayesha can only guess why.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi line up her daily and career choices with environmental impact?
qa.a: Steel lunch boxes and cycling in daily life, asking about waste at work, and moving to a textile recycling job.

qa.q: How has Lakshmi's change affected Ayesha?
qa.a: Ayesha has started checking the labels on her own clothes, quietly influenced even without knowing all Lakshmi's reasons.

grounding: A colleague observes a young woman align her daily habits and then her career with lower environmental impact.

passage:
January. Aditi and Anand opened the first electricity bill for their new Chennai flat and laughed at how big it was: two ACs, a geyser left on all day, lights in empty rooms. Aditi, who worked in climate research, felt like a hypocrite.
March. They put a paper chart on the fridge and noted the meter every Sunday. Anand set the ACs to twenty-six degrees with the ceiling fan on, and they put the geyser on a timer. They argued about the dryer and settled on drying clothes on the balcony except in the monsoon.
October. Their bill had fallen by a third. Harder was the wedding in Singapore in December: flying felt wrong, not going felt worse. They decided to go, but Aditi would replace two work trips with video calls, and they stopped pretending small switches cancelled everything. "We're not perfect," Anand said. "We're paying attention."

qa.q: What temperature did Anand set the ACs to?
qa.a: Twenty-six degrees.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling on seeing the first electricity bill?
qa.a: Aditi felt like a hypocrite, uncomfortable that their home didn't match Aditi's climate work.

qa.q: What made their approach realistic rather than guilt-driven?
qa.a: Weekly meter tracking, specific changes, and honest trade-offs like going to the wedding but cutting work flights.

qa.q: How does Anand see their efforts?
qa.a: Anand sees them as imperfect but attentive, comfortable with steady progress rather than purity.

grounding: Over a year, a young couple track and cut their household energy use and make honest trade-offs about flying.

passage: Gargi, you ask how I chose my career. Sit, let your Tanvir Chacha tell you. When I was twenty-five, two letters came in the same week. One from a thermal power company in Singrauli: good salary, a house with the job. The other from a small government lab in Pune testing solar cookers: half the pay, a room shared with another engineer. Everyone told me to take the power job. My father had borrowed for my degree. I went to Singrauli for the interview. I saw the ash ponds, grey for kilometres, and children coughing in the colony. I came back and took the solar lab. Some years were hard. Your Chachi and I lived small, and I cycled everywhere, not only for the planet but because we had no car. Forty years later, I can say my work left something good behind. You don't have to choose as I did, Gargi. Just look at what your work leaves behind.

qa.q: Where was the thermal power company?
qa.a: In Singrauli.

qa.q: What was young Tanvir feeling after seeing the ash ponds?
qa.a: Tanvir felt disturbed and unsettled by the grey ponds and coughing children, which changed his mind.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Tanvir's choice, and what did it cost?
qa.a: Seeing the ash ponds at the interview; Tanvir chose the solar lab, at half the salary and with years of living small.

qa.q: How might Tanvir's father have felt about the choice?
qa.a: His father, who had borrowed for the degree, was probably worried and disappointed at the lower pay.

grounding: An uncle tells a young woman how, at twenty-five, he chose a lower-paid career for its environmental impact.

passage: Vandana, you asked what I want my daughter to keep from our side. I think about it every night while feeding her. Me, Charu, the girl who rolled her eyes at every puja. First, Konkani. My Aaji's lullabies are in Konkani, and if I don't speak it to her, it ends with me. So I talk to her in Konkani, even badly. Second, the Chaturthi modaks, because making them is how our whole family sits together. Third, Aaji's habit of feeding whoever comes to the door. But some things I'm dropping. Nobody will keep my daughter out of the kitchen at certain times of the month. Nobody will count gold for her wedding. When my mother asked if I was "picking and choosing" our culture, I said yes. Every generation does. I'm just doing it on purpose.

qa.q: Which language does Charu speak to her daughter?
qa.a: Konkani.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling when her mother asked about picking and choosing?
qa.a: Charu felt confident and settled, answering that every generation chooses and she is simply doing it on purpose.

qa.q: How did Charu decide what heritage to keep?
qa.a: She kept what connects the family and carries meaning, like Konkani, modaks and feeding guests, and dropped customs that limit or burden her daughter.

qa.q: How might Charu's mother feel about these choices?
qa.a: Her mother may feel uneasy that some customs are being dropped, yet reassured that the language and festivals will continue.

grounding: A young mother tells a friend which language, food and values she will pass on and which customs she will drop.

passage: I'm Arnab, and I've lived across the landing from Sunaina in our Delhi building for three years. I don't know what made her start, but I watched it grow. Last Bihu she was homesick, I think; she played old Bihu songs loudly on her balcony. The building's kids gathered, curious. The next week there was a hand-written sign in the lift: "Assamese songs and stories, Sunday 5 p.m., terrace, free." Six children came. Then eleven. She taught them one song, then the meaning of every line, then how her grandmother made pithas for the harvest. She didn't insist they be Assamese; my own son is from a Bengali family and now sings better than I do. She also asked the kids to bring songs from their own families, and one Sunday was all Malayalam and Punjabi. I think she decided heritage survives if you share it, not just if you guard it.

qa.q: How many children came the first week?
qa.a: Six children.

qa.q: What might Sunaina have been feeling when she played Bihu songs loudly on the balcony?
qa.a: Sunaina was probably homesick and missing home at festival time, though Arnab can only guess.

qa.q: What makes Sunaina's way of passing on heritage work?
qa.a: She teaches meanings and stories along with the songs, welcomes children of any background, and invites them to share their own families' songs.

qa.q: How does Arnab see the terrace sessions?
qa.a: Arnab watches them grow with interest and warmth, is pleased that Arnab's own son sings the songs, and guesses Sunaina believes sharing keeps heritage alive.

grounding: A neighbour describes a young woman passing on Assamese songs and stories to children of many backgrounds.

passage:
The day after Ammamma's funeral. Lakshmi and her sister Seema sat among Ammamma's things in the Vijayawada house: brass lamps, a notebook of recipes in Telugu, a tin of rangoli powder. Seema wanted to keep everything. Lakshmi, who lived in Bengaluru and barely cooked, felt guilty for wanting almost nothing.
Two weeks later. On a video call they made a list. Lakshmi would keep the recipe notebook and learn three dishes properly. Seema would keep the lamps and draw the muggulu every Sankranti. They agreed they would not keep Ammamma's rule that daughters-in-law ate last.
Sankranti, three months later. Seema sent a photo of her muggulu, crooked but full. In her Bengaluru kitchen, Lakshmi made Ammamma's pesarattu from the notebook and sent a voice note to her niece describing, in Telugu, how Ammamma used to flip it with her bare fingers.

qa.q: What was in Ammamma's notebook?
qa.a: Recipes in Telugu.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling the day after the funeral?
qa.a: Lakshmi was grieving and felt guilty for wanting almost nothing of Ammamma's things.

qa.q: How did the sisters decide what to preserve?
qa.a: They divided what each could truly carry on, like the recipes and the muggulu, and chose to drop the rule that daughters-in-law ate last.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi's niece experience the voice note?
qa.a: The niece would likely feel connected to a great-grandmother she may barely remember, hearing the story in Telugu.

grounding: After their grandmother's death, two sisters decide over months which rituals, recipes and values to carry on.

passage:
The Friday of the funeral. Afreen stood at the back of the crowded hall while person after person spoke about Urmila Ma'am, the professor who had supervised her master's. Nobody mentioned her publications. They talked about how she answered every student's email by midnight, and taught the watchman's daughter maths on Saturdays. Afreen went home and couldn't sleep. What would people say about her?
Two weeks later. The dread had turned into questions. She wrote in her notebook: What would I want to have done, if I had ten years? Twenty? The answers surprised her. Not the promotion. Teaching. Her sister's children. Her father's stories, recorded before they were lost.
Three months later. Afreen was tutoring two girls from her building on Sundays and recording her father's village stories every Friday evening. She still thought about death sometimes, but now with a calmer, almost practical feeling: then let me use the time.

qa.q: What did Urmila Ma'am teach the watchman's daughter?
qa.a: Maths, on Saturdays.

qa.q: How did Afreen's feelings change from the funeral to three months later?
qa.a: At first Afreen felt restless dread and couldn't sleep; later she felt calmer and practical, letting the thought of death guide how she used her time.

qa.q: What did Afreen's notebook questions help her do?
qa.a: Imagining ten or twenty years left showed what mattered, teaching, family and her father's stories, so she acted on them.

qa.q: How might Afreen's father feel being recorded every Friday?
qa.a: Her father would probably feel valued and touched that his village stories are being kept.

grounding: After a mentor's funeral, a young woman faces mortality and reshapes her time around what will outlast her.

passage: Sonali, you're asking why I still go to the library every morning at eighty. Let your Kalyani Paati tell you. When I was twenty-six, my dearest friend Revathi fell ill and died within a year. We were the same age. Before she went, she asked me to water the neem saplings she had planted outside the village school. I did it for months, crying into the bucket. And I kept thinking: if I went tomorrow, what would I leave? Some saris, some recipes. That frightened me more than death itself. So I started small. I collected twenty old books from neighbours and put them on a shelf in the temple verandah, with a notebook for borrowing. Then fifty books. Then a room. Revathi's neems are big trees now, shading the library door. I'm not afraid of dying, Sonali. I'm only afraid of wasting the mornings.

qa.q: What did Revathi ask Kalyani to water?
qa.a: The neem saplings outside the village school.

qa.q: What was young Kalyani feeling while watering the saplings?
qa.a: Kalyani felt deep grief, crying into the bucket, and a growing fear of leaving little behind.

qa.q: What was Kalyani's turning point, and how did it shape her legacy?
qa.a: Asking what she would leave if she died tomorrow; she started a small shelf of books that grew into the village library.

qa.q: How might Revathi have felt asking Kalyani to water the trees?
qa.a: Revathi was probably facing her death with care for what she had started, trusting her dearest friend to carry it on.

grounding: A grandmother tells how, at twenty-six, her friend's death led her to build a library as her legacy.

passage: The visa appointment for Parveen's new job in Dubai was nine days away when her father's scan results came back. The doctors spoke gently: months, perhaps a year. That night, on the hospital's plastic chairs, Parveen felt a cold dread, and then an odd clarity. Anirban, her fiancé, brought tea and sat beside her. "A year from now, what will you wish you had done?" he asked. She knew at once. She would wish she had been here. She would also wish she hadn't thrown away the job Abbu was so proud of. They planned through the night. Parveen asked the company to defer her joining by six months; they agreed to four. She moved back into her old room. She recorded Abbu telling stories about his tailoring shop, and he taught her to stitch buttonholes, laughing at her crooked ones. When she finally flew out, Abbu, thinner, came to the airport and slipped his old scissors into her bag.

qa.q: How many days away was the visa appointment?
qa.a: Nine days.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling on the hospital chairs that night?
qa.a: Parveen felt a cold dread, then an unexpected clarity about what mattered.

qa.q: How did Anirban's question help Parveen decide?
qa.a: Imagining her regrets a year ahead showed she wanted both to be with Abbu and to keep the job, which led to asking for a deferral.

qa.q: How might Abbu feel teaching Parveen buttonholes?
qa.a: Abbu would likely feel joy and pride, passing on his craft and sharing laughter in a hard time.

grounding: Facing her father's terminal illness and a job deadline, a young woman chooses time and legacy with him while keeping her future.

passage:
Monday, 6:30 a.m.
Day one after the gap. For two years I sat every morning for fifteen minutes: first the Hanuman Chalisa the way Nani taught me, then silence, just breathing. Then the new job started in January, and I "skipped just today" for six weeks.
And I've been snappier. With Eshaan, with the auto driver, with myself. Last night Eshaan said, gently, "You were calmer when you did your morning thing." I was annoyed, because he was right.
So today I sat again. My mind was a market. I lost the thread of the Chalisa twice. It didn't matter. The point was never perfect focus; it was coming back.
New rule: if fifteen minutes isn't possible, five. Never zero. And before I touch my phone.
The kettle's whistling. Eshaan's awake. I feel steadier than I have in weeks.
— Deepika

qa.q: How long did Deepika sit every morning before the gap?
qa.a: Fifteen minutes.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when Eshaan mentioned the morning practice?
qa.a: Deepika felt annoyed at first, because he was right that things had been calmer before.

qa.q: What changes will help Deepika sustain the practice?
qa.a: Allowing five minutes when fifteen isn't possible, never zero, and sitting before touching the phone.

qa.q: How might Eshaan have experienced the six weeks without the practice?
qa.a: Eshaan probably felt the snappiness and missed the calmer mornings, which is why he mentioned it gently.

grounding: A young woman's diary records returning to a lapsed daily prayer and meditation practice with simpler rules.

passage: In the drought year, Madhav woke before the sun in their village near Latur and walked the edge of his father's cotton fields in silence. No phone, no radio, just the crunch of dry soil and the first birds. He had learned the practice from a retired teacher at his college hostel: walk slowly, count ten breaths, notice one thing you have never seen before. For two years he had done it every day. This year, with the well low and loan payments looming, it was the only hour his chest wasn't tight. Devika, who taught at the zilla parishad school and walked past to catch her bus, asked one morning what he was doing. "Nothing," he said. "That's the point." She laughed, then joined him the next Sunday. By summer, four people walked the field edge at dawn, mostly silent. The drought didn't lift. But Madhav stopped shouting at his father about money.

qa.q: Where did Madhav walk each morning?
qa.a: The edge of his father's cotton fields.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling during the drought year apart from the walk?
qa.a: Madhav felt tense and anxious, with the well low and loan payments looming; the walk was his only calm hour.

qa.q: What made Madhav's practice last through a hard year?
qa.a: It was simple and daily, walking slowly, counting ten breaths and noticing one new thing without a phone, and he had kept it for two years.

qa.q: How might Devika see the dawn walks?
qa.a: Devika first found the idea amusing, but joining showed her its value, and she became part of a small group.

grounding: In a drought-hit village, a young farmer's long-kept silent walking practice steadies him and draws others in.

passage:
"You're avoiding the health check again," Avni said, spotting the office email still marked unread.
Gopika sighed. "I'm twenty-five. I'm fine."
"Your mother had to start diabetes medicines at forty. And your Ammamma before her."
"That's them."
"That's your family history. Doctors ask about it for a reason."
Gopika stirred her tea. "What if they find something?"
"Then you know early, when it's easier to deal with. Isn't that better than finding out later?"
"You sound like my mother."
"Your mother would be proud of me." Avni grinned. "The office does it free. I'll book us both for the same morning."
"And you'll hold my hand for the blood test?"
"I'll hold your bag. Your hand is your problem."
Gopika laughed, opened the email and clicked register. "Fine. But you're buying breakfast after."

qa.q: At what age did Gopika's mother start diabetes medicines?
qa.a: At forty.

qa.q: What was Gopika worried about in going for the check?
qa.a: Gopika felt anxious that the check might find something.

qa.q: Why is family history a good reason to go for a check-up?
qa.a: It can show a risk early, when it is easier to manage, instead of discovering it later.

qa.q: How does Avni see Gopika's avoidance?
qa.a: Avni sees fear behind it and responds with humour and practical help, booking them both together.

grounding: A friend helps a young woman with a family history of diabetes take up a preventive health check.

passage: When Papa had his heart attack at fifty-two, I, Jatin, was twenty-four and sure it had nothing to do with me. He survived, thank God. In the hospital corridor the cardiologist asked me, not him, "Have you had your own checks?" I laughed. She didn't. She said heart problems can run in families, and early checks are how you catch things while they're small. I still didn't go for three months. What finally moved me was Farida, my wife, who simply booked two slots at the clinic and said, "We're doing this together, like the dentist." The results were mostly fine. My cholesterol was a little high, and the doctor talked about food, walking and checking again later. It wasn't dramatic. But now I know my numbers, Papa and I walk together on Sunday mornings, and I've stopped pretending family history is someone else's story.

qa.q: How old was Papa when he had his heart attack?
qa.a: Fifty-two.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling when the cardiologist asked about his own checks?
qa.a: Jatin felt dismissive and a bit amused, sure it had nothing to do with him.

qa.q: What finally got Jatin to the clinic, and why did it work?
qa.a: Farida booking two slots and treating it as a shared routine, like the dentist, which removed the excuse and the fear of going alone.

qa.q: How might Papa feel about the Sunday walks?
qa.a: Papa probably feels glad and closer to his son, sharing a healthy habit after his scare.

grounding: A young man looks back on taking his family's heart risk seriously and starting preventive checks with his wife.

passage: Occupational health nurse's note, annual screening week. Uday (logistics) came without a reminder, which is rare in his age group. He brought a written list: his father's high blood pressure, his mother's thyroid condition, a grandfather who had a stroke young. He said his colleague Anjali had made him write it after her own screening caught something early. His results today were within the normal range, and he looked almost disappointed. "So I did all this for nothing?" I explained that a normal result now gives us a baseline to compare with later, which is the whole point. I referred him to the company doctor to discuss what his family history means for future checks, rather than guessing himself. He asked for copies of his results to keep in a folder at home. I'll suggest the family-history list to the whole team. — Sister Mary, occupational health

qa.q: What did Uday bring to the screening?
qa.a: A written list of his family's health history.

qa.q: What might Uday have been feeling when he asked 'So I did all this for nothing?'
qa.a: Uday seemed a little deflated, as if a normal result made the effort feel wasted.

qa.q: Why is a normal result still useful, according to the note?
qa.a: It gives a baseline to compare with later, and his family history can guide the doctor's advice on future checks.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel knowing Uday made the list because of her?
qa.a: Anjali would likely feel glad, and a bit proud, that sharing her own early catch encouraged a colleague.

grounding: A nurse's note shows a young man tracking his family health risks and using screening as a baseline.

passage:
"I cried in the supermarket today," Afreen admitted, dropping onto a kitchen chair in their Berlin flat. "Over coriander. They sell it in these tiny sad bunches."
Tenzin laughed, not unkindly. "Month three?"
"Month four."
"Month four is the worst. I cried over momo wrappers."
"How long did it last?"
"Until I stopped trying to be either fully German or fully from Dharamshala." Tenzin put the kettle on. "I joined a climbing club with Germans. And I found three Tibetan families who do Losar together. Both."
"I don't know anyone."
"You know me. And the Indian grocery near the U-Bahn has proper coriander on Fridays."
Afreen smiled weakly. "You're joking."
"Never joke about coriander." Tenzin handed her a mug. "Eid's next month. Invite people. Germans, Indians, whoever. Make your Ammi's sheer khurma."
"In this tiny kitchen?"
"Especially in this tiny kitchen."

qa.q: What made Afreen cry in the supermarket?
qa.a: Coriander sold in tiny sad bunches.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling in month four?
qa.a: Afreen felt homesick and lonely, crying over small reminders of home.

qa.q: How did Tenzin build belonging, and what does Tenzin suggest to Afreen?
qa.a: Tenzin joined a local climbing club and a Tibetan community; for Afreen, Tenzin suggests an Eid meal with guests of all backgrounds, keeping her identity while making connections.

qa.q: How does Tenzin see Afreen's tears?
qa.a: Tenzin sees them as a normal stage, having cried over momo wrappers too, and responds with warmth and practical tips.

grounding: A flatmate who adapted to Berlin helps a homesick young woman build belonging without losing her identity.

passage: When I, Suraj, moved from Patna to Singapore for work, I thought the hard part would be the job. It was the silence. Nobody on my floor talked in the lift. At the office, people ate lunch at their desks. I missed shouting across the lane to my neighbour. For months I was polite and invisible. Aparna, my wife, joined me in the second year and changed things. She said good morning to the cleaner, Auntie Lim, who turned out to have a son studying in Chennai. She found the Bihari association that celebrated Chhath at the beach, with thekua and everything. I went reluctantly and stood waist-deep in the sea at sunrise, holding the soop, among forty families from home. I cried a bit. Back at work, I joined a colleague's Friday lunch group, learned their jokes, and taught them the word "jugaad". I'm both now. Some days it tires me. Most days it feels like more.

qa.q: What did the Bihari association celebrate at the beach?
qa.a: Chhath.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling in the first months in Singapore?
qa.a: Suraj felt lonely and invisible, missing the noise and closeness of home.

qa.q: What helped Suraj adapt while keeping his identity?
qa.a: Aparna's small friendly contacts, finding the Bihari association for Chhath, and joining a colleague's lunch group.

qa.q: How might Auntie Lim see Aparna's greetings?
qa.a: Auntie Lim probably felt noticed and warmed, which is how they found a connection through her son in Chennai.

grounding: A young man looks back on adapting to life in Singapore while keeping his Bihari identity through community.

passage:
January. Darshan started at an architecture firm in Ahmedabad and, within two weeks, missed two deadlines and lost a site measurement sheet. He had been diagnosed with ADHD at nineteen, and he knew the pattern: open-plan noise, a dozen small tasks, nothing written down.
February. He spent a Sunday designing systems the way he'd design a building. One notebook, always in his left pocket. Every task written the moment it was given. Noise-cancelling headphones for drawing hours. A ten-minute walk after lunch, because his energy crashed at two. He told his manager, Jagdish, what he needed: written instructions after site visits, and deadlines split into smaller checkpoints. Jagdish said, "Honestly, that helps me too."
June. Darshan hadn't missed a deadline in three months. He still lost pens constantly. He had started laughing about it and now bought them in packs of fifty.

qa.q: What did Darshan keep in his left pocket?
qa.a: One notebook.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling after missing two deadlines in January?
qa.a: Darshan was probably frustrated and discouraged, recognising an old pattern.

qa.q: Which systems fit Darshan's attention and energy patterns?
qa.a: Writing every task in one notebook, headphones for focus, a walk after lunch for the energy crash, and asking for written instructions and smaller checkpoints.

qa.q: How does Jagdish see Darshan's requests?
qa.a: Jagdish finds them reasonable and even helpful personally, suggesting the changes improve the whole team's work.

grounding: Over months, a young architect with ADHD builds work systems that fit his attention and energy.

passage: Sunaina, you asked how I survive the office parties. Let your Joseph Uncle tell you what I learned at twenty-five, long before anyone had words for people like me. I was a draughtsman in Kochi, good with lines, bad with noise. The tube lights buzzed like bees, and by lunch every day I had a headache and snapped at people. I thought I was just difficult. Then my senior, an old man called Varghese, noticed I worked best at six in the morning, before anyone came. He let me start early and leave early. So I built my own rules. Dark glasses under tube lights. Cotton in my ears on the bus. Parties: arrive first, leave after one hour, while I still liked everyone. My wife learned my signal, a touch to my ear: time to go home. People called me strange. I called it knowing myself. Build your own rules, Sunaina.

qa.q: What time did Joseph work best?
qa.a: At six in the morning, before anyone came.

qa.q: What was young Joseph feeling by lunch each day?
qa.a: Joseph felt overwhelmed and irritable, with a headache from the noise and lights.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what systems grew from it?
qa.a: Varghese letting him start early; Joseph then built rules like dark glasses, cotton in his ears on the bus, and leaving parties after an hour.

qa.q: How might Varghese have seen young Joseph?
qa.a: Varghese seems to have seen a skilled worker who needed quiet, not a difficult one, and cared enough to adjust his hours.

grounding: An older man tells a young woman how, at twenty-five, he built life and work systems around his sensory sensitivity.

passage: Irawati's promotion came in November, just before her cousin's week-long wedding in Amritsar. The new role meant back-to-back video meetings; the wedding meant five days of dhol, crowds and relatives' questions. By the second evening of the sangeet she was shaking, and slipped out to the car park with her hands over her ears. Gurpreet, her husband, found her there. He didn't ask what was wrong; he knew her pattern. Loud, bright, long days drained her in a way that sleep alone didn't fix. They made a plan right there. She would go to the ceremonies that mattered most and skip the late-night dancing. Earplugs in her purse. A quiet hour in the hotel room each afternoon. And back at work, she would ask her manager to cluster meetings in the mornings, keeping afternoons for focused work. Her Bua raised an eyebrow at the early exits. Irawati smiled, touched her arm, and left anyway.

qa.q: Where was the cousin's wedding?
qa.a: In Amritsar.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling in the car park?
qa.a: Irawati felt overwhelmed and drained, shaking with her hands over her ears.

qa.q: What plan fitted Irawati's energy and sensory patterns?
qa.a: Choosing the most important ceremonies, carrying earplugs, taking a quiet hour each afternoon, and clustering work meetings in the mornings.

qa.q: How might Irawati's Bua see the early exits?
qa.a: Bua raised an eyebrow, probably finding it odd or impolite, not knowing how draining the noise is for Irawati.

grounding: Facing a big wedding and a demanding new role, a young woman plans around her own sensory and energy limits.
